items.title: 13.3 The bond strength of halogen molecules

source_refs.note: Topic 13.3 with Table 13.3 and the F2 drawing (printed as a second Figure 13.1), printed page 294.

blocks.text: Bond strength in the halogens decreases down the group from chlorine to iodine, because the increasing atomic size gives longer bond lengths and weaker bonds; the bond energy falls gradually from Cl2 to I2. Fluorine is the exception: its bond is relatively weak because fluorine atoms are very small, so there is significant repulsion between the lone pairs on the two atoms (Figure 13.1 shows the F2 molecule with its lone pairs), which weakens the bond despite fluorine's high electronegativity.

blocks.prompt: The F-F bond is weaker than the Cl-Cl bond although fluorine is the most electronegative element. Explain (Quick Check 13.2a; MCQ I).
blocks.explanation: The F-F bond is very short because the atoms are tiny, so the three lone pairs on each fluorine are brought close to those on the other and repel strongly; this repulsion offsets the attraction of the shared pair and lowers the bond energy to 156 kJ mol-1. Chlorine atoms are larger, the lone pairs are farther apart, and Cl2 has the strongest bond of the group at 243 kJ mol-1.

items: X-X bond energy falls Cl2 (243) to Br2 (193) to I2 (151 kJ mol-1) as atoms get larger; F2 (156) is anomalously weak because lone-pair repulsion between the tiny atoms weakens the bond.
